passages.title: Carbon dioxide (Scully et al., 2019; NASA, 2023)
passages.excerpt: Twenty-two astronaut-like volunteers were exposed for a few hours to 600 to 5,000 ppm. There was no clear dose-response pattern in decision-making or cognition. Longer exposures still need study. NASA reports that 19 of 49 astronauts in one ISS analysis had headaches, and that carbon dioxide level was linked to them. Fluid shifts in microgravity can cause similar symptoms.
passages.tracking: Record headaches or slowed thinking, and check the vehicle’s cabin alerts.

sources.title: Effects of acute exposures to carbon dioxide on decision making and cognition in astronaut-like subjects
Carbon dioxide technical brief
sources.journal: NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer

passages.title: Lunar dust (Miranda et al., 2023)
passages.excerpt: Apollo astronauts reported allergy-like symptoms after tracking dust into the lunar module. One reported sneezing, red eyes, an itchy throat and congested sinuses. Researchers are also concerned about effects on the lungs, skin and eyes.
passages.tracking: Record breathing, eye or throat symptoms after surface work.

sources.title: A Dusty Road for Astronauts

passages.title: Microbes on cabin surfaces (Avila-Herrera et al., 2020)
passages.excerpt: A study of one crew member found that ISS surfaces resemble the crew’s skin microbes. The authors support continued microbial surveillance for long missions.
passages.tracking: Follow habitat hygiene procedures and report shared symptoms.

sources.title: Crewmember microbiome may influence microbial composition of ISS habitable surfaces

passages.title: Air, water and surfaces (Urbaniak et al., 2022; Novikova et al., 2006)
passages.excerpt: ISS surface microbes are mostly human skin organisms, with Staphylococcus and Malassezia the most represented. A six-year survey found Staphylococcus dominant in air and surface samples. No viable pathogens were recovered from potable water.
passages.tracking: Follow cabin cleaning and water sampling procedures.

sources.title: Microbial Tracking-2, a metagenomics analysis of bacteria and fungi onboard the International Space Station
Survey of environmental biocontamination on board the International Space Station

passages.title: Noise, vibration and light (Tomsia et al., 2024)
passages.excerpt: Astronauts often have disturbed body clocks and poor sleep. Reviewers recommend designing stations with less noise and vibration, and with lighting that supports the circadian rhythm.
passages.tracking: Record whether noise or lighting affected your sleep.

sources.title: Long-term space missions’ effects on the human organism: what we do know and what requires further research

passages.title: Food and nutrition (Pittia et al., 2023)
passages.excerpt: Too few calories have contributed to muscle loss and weakened immune and cardiovascular systems during missions. Prolonged storage can degrade nutrients. There is currently no reliable way to measure total energy use in real time, so diet and body mass need monitoring.
passages.tracking: Record appetite changes and intake against the meal plan.

sources.title: Unraveling the intricate connection between dietary factors and the success in long-term space missions

passages.title: Calories in early spaceflight (Altman & Fisher, 1986)
passages.excerpt: Early missions assumed weightlessness needed fewer calories, but tasks that use friction on Earth take muscular effort in space. Apollo crews averaged 1,877 kcal a day against about 2,900 recommended and lost a mean 3.9 kg. U.S. space diets rose from about 2,500 to about 3,000 kcal a day. On the 13-day Apollo 17, intake fell short of needs and each crew member lost a mean 1 kg of lean body mass and 2.3 kg of fat. Unpalatable early foods were often not fully eaten.
passages.tracking: Record what is actually eaten, including snacks.

passages.title: Diet and weight loss on Skylab (Altman & Fisher, 1986)
passages.excerpt: Of the nine Skylab crew, the five who ate less in flight lost 75% more weight than those who kept their preflight intake. About 60% of the weight lost was lean body mass. Skylab 4, with the most food and exercise, was the only flight with no net tissue loss. Analyses suggest losses can be prevented with about 46 to 50 kcal per kg of body weight a day, plus 5 to 6 kcal per kg of exercise.
passages.tracking: Track body mass and food intake together.

passages.title: Short sleep (Jones et al., 2022; Flynn-Evans et al., 2016)
passages.excerpt: In 24 astronauts on six-month ISS missions, average sleep was about 6.5 hours. Sleeping under 6 hours was linked to slower responses, more stress and higher workload. Longer sleep helped. Sleep medication is also common in flight.
passages.tracking: Track sleep hours, stress and workload every day.

Circadian misalignment affects sleep and medication use before and during spaceflight

passages.title: Depression and cognition (Yin et al., 2023)
passages.excerpt: The combined stress of long missions, including microgravity, isolation, noise and disrupted body clocks, could contribute to depression and cognitive impairment.
passages.tracking: Discuss lasting changes in mood, motivation or focus privately with the medical officer.

sources.title: Long-term spaceflight composite stress induces depression and cognitive impairment in astronauts: insights from neuroplasticity

passages.title: Isolation and confinement (Choukér & Stahn, 2020; Gatti et al., 2022)
passages.excerpt: Spaceflight analogs are used to study how prolonged isolation affects the brain, behavior and immune system. Stress, coping, adaptation and resilience can each be affected differently.
passages.tracking: Keep check-ins consistent so changes are easier to notice.

sources.title: COVID-19: the largest isolation study in history: the value of shared learnings from spaceflight analogs
Affective health and countermeasures in long-duration space exploration

passages.title: Team dynamics (Bell et al., 2019)
passages.excerpt: A review of 72 analog sources, such as Antarctic stations and space chambers, examined how crews work together. All teams reported at least one conflict by 90 days or 40% of the mission. Mood data did not consistently support a morale dip after the mission’s halfway point, known as the third-quarter phenomenon.
passages.tracking: Use the crew connection score in the daily check-in.

sources.title: What We Know About Team Dynamics for Long-Distance Space Missions: A Systematic Review of Analog Research

passages.title: Loneliness (Cantisani et al., 2026)
passages.excerpt: Twelve crew members at an Antarctic station were followed for 10 months with surveys and wearable proximity sensors. Loneliness and conflict rose while cohesion and performance fell. More close-range contact was linked to more conflict, so contact alone did not equal support.
passages.tracking: Discuss loneliness privately with the medical officer. Wearable sensors are not part of ORBIT.

sources.title: Social interactions in isolated, confined, and extreme environments: A study of Antarctic winter teams using wearable sensors

passages.title: Delayed contact with Earth (Pagnini, 2024; Smith, 2024)
passages.excerpt: Communication delays, isolation and confinement can affect mental health. Automated support has been proposed for times when Earth cannot respond quickly, with benefits, drawbacks and unknowns still to be worked out.
passages.tracking: Plan what the crew will do while waiting for a reply.

sources.title: Supporting the Mind in Space: Psychological Tools for Long-Duration Missions
Automated Psychotherapy in a Spaceflight Environment: Advantages, Drawbacks, and Unknowns

passages.title: Cognitive testing (Casario et al., 2022)
passages.excerpt: The Cognition battery of 10 brief tests was built for astronauts. Its acceptability was evaluated in 87 people on the ISS and in space analog settings on Earth.
passages.tracking: Repeated cognitive tests are not yet part of ORBIT.

sources.title: Acceptability of the Cognition Test Battery in astronaut and astronaut-surrogate populations

passages.title: Isolation in analog habitats (NASA, 2024)
passages.excerpt: NASA notes that sleep loss, body-clock disruption and work overload on long, isolated missions may lower performance and harm health, so crews are carefully chosen, trained and supported. Its analogs include HERA, a 650-square-foot habitat where crews live for 45 days, and CHAPEA, a 1,700-square-foot habitat for simulated year-long Mars stays with four crew.
passages.tracking: Log sleep, workload and mood across the mission.

passages.title: Mood over long stays (Bell et al., 2026)
passages.excerpt: The APEX psychology suite was given to 121 people in 40 teams: astronauts in space for 150 to 350 days and analog crews isolated for 45 to 240 days. No one showed clinically elevated depression. Positive mood declined over time, while negative mood and stress varied widely and tracked situational stressors more than time in isolation. These are summary results from a conference abstract.
passages.tracking: Note stressful events alongside mood check-ins.

passages.title: Morale in the third quarter (Stuster, 2010)
passages.excerpt: Personal journals from astronauts on six-month ISS expeditions were mostly about work, then outside communications, adjustment, crew interactions and recreation. Morale declined in the third quarter of the missions. Astronauts said journal writing helped them keep perspective, and living on the ISS was less difficult than they had expected.
passages.tracking: Check in more often during the third quarter of a long mission.

passages.title: Distance from Earth (NASA, 2024; McBrayer et al., 2022)
passages.excerpt: Mars is on average 140 million miles from Earth, and a Mars mission would keep crews away for about three years. NASA cites one-way communication delays of up to 20 minutes. A Mars mission analysis found delays of 0 to 22 minutes over a mission, and disruptions lasting from several days to several months depending on the communication band.
passages.tracking: Keep emergency procedures available without a link to Earth.

passages.title: Acting without ground support (Parisi et al., 2023)
passages.excerpt: An analysis of real ISS and Apollo anomalies found that even delays of seconds to a minute hamper the ground’s real-time oversight and its ability to catch fast-moving problems. With delays of up to 40 minutes on Mars missions, crews must make time-critical decisions on their own. The authors note that the effectiveness of countermeasures is still a research gap.
passages.tracking: Rehearse decisions the crew may have to make alone.

passages.title: Cancer risk (Guo et al., 2022; Chancellor et al., 2014; Barcellos-Hoff et al., 2015)
passages.excerpt: Cell and animal experiments show that high-energy protons and heavy ions can cause cancer. There are no human data on extended exposure to these complex radiation fields, so the size of the risk to astronauts remains very uncertain.
passages.tracking: Track cumulative dose against the mission limit.

Space Radiation: The Number One Risk to Astronaut Health beyond Low Earth Orbit
Concepts and challenges in cancer risk prediction for the space radiation environment

passages.title: Brain and nervous system (Chancellor et al., 2014; Kokhan & Dobynde, 2023)
passages.excerpt: Space radiation may affect the central nervous system, but the evidence is mixed. Rodent and primate experiments show negative, neutral and even positive effects on cognition at space-related doses.
passages.tracking: Record changes in memory, focus or mood.

The Effects of Galactic Cosmic Rays on the Central Nervous System: From Negative to Unexpectedly Positive Effects That Astronauts May Encounter

passages.title: Long-term tissue damage (Chancellor et al., 2014; Vernice et al., 2020)
passages.excerpt: Degenerative tissue effects are one of the main radiation risks beyond low Earth orbit. Exposure to deep space radiation has been linked to artery degeneration, aortic stiffness and faster atherosclerosis.
passages.tracking: Track cumulative dose and keep long-term follow-up records.

sources.title: Space Radiation: The Number One Risk to Astronaut Health beyond Low Earth Orbit
Long-term spaceflight and the cardiovascular system

passages.title: Acute radiation syndrome (Kennedy, 2014; Chancellor et al., 2014)
passages.excerpt: A major solar particle event could put astronauts at significant risk of acute radiation syndrome, which other spaceflight stressors may worsen. Shielding is an effective countermeasure against these events.
passages.tracking: Follow the vehicle’s radiation procedure. Report unexplained nausea or fatigue after a solar event.

Space Radiation: The Number One Risk to Astronaut Health beyond Low Earth Orbit

passages.title: Cataracts (Cucinotta et al., 2001)
passages.excerpt: Among 295 astronauts, those with higher lens doses (above 8 mSv) had more cataracts. The authors call the results preliminary because the scoring methods were subjective.
passages.tracking: Record vision changes and keep eye exam results for follow-up.

sources.title: Space Radiation and Cataracts in Astronauts

passages.title: Radiation limits (NASA, 2022)
passages.excerpt: NASA limits career effective dose to under 600 mSv for all ages and sexes, and exposure to 250 mSv per solar particle event. NASA also requires space weather monitoring, radiation alerting and dose monitoring.
passages.tracking: Enter dosimeter readings. ORBIT cannot measure radiation.

sources.journal: NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer

passages.title: Secondary radiation (Chancellor et al., 2014)
passages.excerpt: Space radiation striking spacecraft shielding produces secondary particles, including neutrons. These can deliver a significant share of the total mission dose.
passages.tracking: Follow the vehicle’s shielding and shelter procedure.

sources.title: Space Radiation: The Number One Risk to Astronaut Health beyond Low Earth Orbit

passages.title: Light flashes (Fuglesang et al., 2006)
passages.excerpt: Of 59 astronauts who answered a survey, 47 noticed flashes of light during spaceflight, most often before sleep. They are related to high-energy particles, and several people thought they disturbed their sleep.
passages.tracking: Note disturbed sleep in the daily check-in.

sources.title: Phosphenes in low Earth orbit: survey responses from 59 astronauts

passages.title: Radiation dose (Apollo 10) (NASA, 1969)
passages.excerpt: Each Apollo 10 crewman received a total absorbed dose of about 0.5 rad, which the report calls well below the medically significant threshold. Passive dosimeters at the chest, thigh and ankle read 386 to 560 millirads. Passing through the Van Allen belts, the highest rates were 3.63 rad/hr skin dose and 2.09 rad/hr depth dose.
passages.tracking: Record dosimeter readings after each pass through high-radiation regions.

passages.title: Dormant virus reactivation (Rooney et al., 2019; Crucian et al., 2018)
passages.excerpt: Dormant herpes viruses reactivate during spaceflight: 53% of shuttle astronauts and 61% of ISS astronauts shed one or more. Shedding is typically symptom-free, though it has been linked to skin lesions in some cases.
passages.tracking: Viral testing needs laboratory equipment. Record cold sores and skin lesions.

sources.title: Herpes Virus Reactivation in Astronauts During Spaceflight and Its Application on Earth
Immune System Dysregulation During Spaceflight: Potential Countermeasures for Deep Space Exploration Missions

passages.title: Altered immune signaling (Crucian et al., 2014)
passages.excerpt: Blood levels of 22 cytokines were monitored in 28 astronauts on long ISS missions. Several rose during flight, suggesting that immune regulation changes in space.
passages.tracking: Immune blood tests are not yet part of ORBIT.

sources.title: Plasma cytokine concentrations indicate that in vivo hormonal regulation of immunity is altered during long-duration spaceflight

passages.title: Rashes and infections (Crucian et al., 2016)
passages.excerpt: Medical records from 46 ISS crew members showed 3.40 immune-related events per flight year. Skin rashes were reported most often, followed by upper respiratory symptoms. Rashes or hypersensitivities made up 40% of notable events.
passages.tracking: Record temperature, new rashes and respiratory symptoms.

sources.title: Incidence of clinical symptoms during long-duration orbital spaceflight

passages.title: Wound healing (Puhl et al., 2022)
passages.excerpt: Research suggests that wound healing is slowed and impaired in microgravity. Radiation and other spaceflight stressors may add to this.
passages.tracking: Track size and warning signs until the wound heals.

sources.title: Wound management and healing in space

passages.title: Skin microbes (Voorhies et al., 2019)
passages.excerpt: In nine astronauts on six to twelve month ISS missions, microbes on the skin, gut, nose and tongue changed. The skin changes might contribute to the high rate of rashes.
passages.tracking: Record skin irritation and how long it lasts.

sources.title: Study of the impact of long-duration space missions at the International Space Station on the astronaut microbiome

passages.title: Skin inflammation (Park et al., 2024)
passages.excerpt: Skin biopsies from the four-person Inspiration4 crew showed raised inflammation-related gene activity after a three-day flight, along with DNA damage and barrier disruption.
passages.tracking: Record redness, dryness or irritation.

sources.title: Spatial multi-omics of human skin reveals KRAS and inflammatory responses to spaceflight

passages.title: Skin fungi (Sugita et al., 2016)
passages.excerpt: In 10 astronauts on half-year ISS stays, skin fungal diversity fell and the share of Malassezia rose. An uncommon yeast was abundant in flight samples from 5 of the 10. Higher colonization is not the same as an infection.
passages.tracking: Flag skin symptoms that persist.

sources.title: Comprehensive analysis of the skin fungal microbiota of astronauts during a half-year stay at the International Space Station

passages.title: Allergy and hypersensitivity (Crucian et al., 2018; Crucian et al., 2016)
passages.excerpt: Some crew members have allergic symptoms and persistent skin hypersensitivity reactions during flight. Longer missions and deep space radiation may increase this clinical risk.
passages.tracking: Record rashes, itching or swelling and what you were exposed to.

sources.title: Immune System Dysregulation During Spaceflight: Potential Countermeasures for Deep Space Exploration Missions
Incidence of clinical symptoms during long-duration orbital spaceflight

passages.title: Fingernail injuries (Opperman et al., 2010)
passages.excerpt: Records from 232 crew members linked fingernail separation to hand size. Hand circumference had the strongest effect on the likelihood of injury from spacesuit gloves.
passages.tracking: Record nail pain, discoloration or separation after spacewalk work.

sources.title: Probability of Spacesuit-Induced Fingernail Trauma Is Associated with Hand Circumference

passages.title: Skin thinning (Neutelings et al., 2015)
passages.excerpt: Mice kept 91 days on the ISS had 15% thinner dermis than matched ground mice. This has not been shown in people.
passages.tracking: Record skin dryness or fragility.

sources.title: Skin physiology in microgravity: a 3-month stay aboard ISS induces dermal atrophy and affects cutaneous muscle and hair follicles cycling in mice

passages.title: Bacteria in flight (Wilson et al., 2007)
passages.excerpt: Salmonella grown on a Space Shuttle mission changed gene expression and was more virulent in mice. This study did not involve infections in crew.
passages.tracking: Follow hygiene procedures and report signs of infection.

sources.title: Space flight alters bacterial gene expression and virulence and reveals a role for global regulator Hfq

passages.title: Lasting gene changes (Garrett-Bakelman et al., 2019)
passages.excerpt: In the one-year NASA Twins Study, most gene expression returned to near preflight levels within six months, but some genes stayed disrupted. This is one astronaut, compared with their identical twin.
passages.tracking: Keep long-term follow-up records after the mission.

sources.title: The NASA Twins Study: A multidimensional analysis of a year-long human spaceflight

passages.title: Bone loss (Man et al., 2022)
passages.excerpt: Microgravity causes 1 to 2% bone loss per month in astronauts, mainly in weight-bearing bones.
passages.tracking: Compare repeated scans from the same site.

sources.title: The effects of microgravity on bone structure and function

passages.title: Back pain and muscle loss (Ceniza-Bordallo et al., 2024)
passages.excerpt: A systematic review of 11 studies found lower back muscle atrophy, reduced range of motion and disc changes. Reports of pain reached 77% during flight, 47% acute after flight and 33% chronic.
passages.tracking: Record back pain and changes in movement.

sources.title: Low Back Pain During and After Spaceflight: A Systematic Review with Meta-Analysis

passages.title: Exercise countermeasures (Jones et al., 2019; Scott et al., 2019)
passages.excerpt: The ISS schedule allows 2.5 hours of exercise a day, and current recommendations combine strength and aerobic training. If that combination is planned poorly, strength gains can be held back, so timing matters.
passages.tracking: Log both aerobic and resistance sessions against the plan.

sources.title: Optimization of Exercise Countermeasures for Human Space Flight: Operational Considerations for Concurrent Strength and Aerobic Training
Introduction to the Frontiers Research Topic: Optimization of Exercise Countermeasures for Human Space Flight

passages.title: Heart and circulation (Vernice et al., 2020; Hoenemann et al., 2023)
passages.excerpt: Fluid shifts toward the head reduce plasma volume by about 10 to 15%. Fainting or near-fainting on standing commonly follows spaceflight. The Hoenemann study is a 60-day bed rest study, not a spaceflight study.
passages.tracking: Track heart rate and blood pressure, and take care when returning to gravity.

Effects of daily artificial gravity training on orthostatic tolerance following 60-day strict head-down tilt bedrest

passages.title: Balance after landing (Clément et al., 2023)
passages.excerpt: On landing day, 28 astronauts performed walking and balance tests at a level comparable to people with bilateral vestibulopathy, a serious balance disorder.
passages.tracking: Plan for impaired balance after any return to gravity.

sources.title: Cognitive and balance functions of astronauts after spaceflight are comparable to those of individuals with bilateral vestibulopathy

passages.title: Heart muscle (Perhonen et al., 2001)
passages.excerpt: In a small study, left ventricle mass fell 8% after six weeks of bed rest. It fell 12% in four astronauts after a 10-day flight, though that change was not statistically significant.
passages.tracking: Keep up the exercise plan and record heart rate and blood pressure.

sources.title: Cardiac atrophy after bed rest and spaceflight

passages.title: Eye changes (Lee et al., 2020)
passages.excerpt: Long microgravity exposure can cause spaceflight-associated neuro-ocular syndrome. Findings include optic disc swelling, globe flattening, retinal folds and shifts toward farsightedness.
passages.tracking: Report near-vision changes. Eye imaging is not part of ORBIT.

sources.title: Spaceflight associated neuro-ocular syndrome (SANS) and the neuro-ophthalmologic effects of microgravity: a review and an update

passages.title: Kidney stones (Pietrzyk et al., 2007)
passages.excerpt: Analysis of 24-hour urine samples showed an increased risk of stone formation after landing. Risk factors can be assessed before flight and right after landing.
passages.tracking: Follow the fluid and diet plan. Report flank pain or urinary symptoms.

sources.title: Renal stone formation among astronauts

passages.title: Changing gravity fields (NASA, 2024)
passages.excerpt: Without Earth’s gravity, weight-bearing bones lose on average 1% to 1.5% of mineral density per month. Fluid shifts toward the head can press on the eyes and affect vision, and dehydration plus calcium leaving the bones can raise kidney stone risk. Moving between gravity fields affects orientation, coordination and balance and can cause space motion sickness. Returning to gravity can cause lightheadedness and fainting.
passages.tracking: Plan for dizziness and balance problems after each gravity change.

passages.title: Heart and circulation after Apollo (Hoffler & Johnson, 1975)
passages.excerpt: Apollo crews had reduced orthostatic tolerance after flight. Heart rate was the most reliable sign: it rose right after flight while systolic and pulse pressure fell. Body weight, calf girth, leg volume and cardiothoracic ratio all decreased and had not fully recovered by the end of postflight testing. Changes varied widely between crew members.
passages.tracking: Compare standing heart rate and blood pressure with preflight values.

passages.title: Motion sickness on Apollo (Homick & Miller, 1975)
passages.excerpt: The larger Apollo command and lunar modules allowed more movement, and vestibular disturbances were more common than on earlier flights. The findings come from motion sickness histories and astronaut reports, because there was no systematic testing program. The authors say in-flight vestibular problems are hard to predict.
passages.tracking: Log nausea or disorientation, especially in the first days of flight.

passages.title: Adapting to weightlessness (Apollo 10) (NASA, 1969)
passages.excerpt: After orbital insertion, all three Apollo 10 crew felt fullness of the head, lasting about 8, 12 and 24 hours. The Lunar Module Pilot had mild vestibular disturbance for the first 2 days and reached the point of nausea within 2 minutes of head-movement exercises. Heart rates during normal activity ranged from 49 to 93 beats/min, rose in critical phases and quickly returned to baseline. No in-flight illnesses occurred.
passages.tracking: Record head fullness and motion sensitivity in the first days.

passages.title: Long-duration findings from Skylab (Johnston & Dietlein, 1975)
passages.excerpt: On Skylab missions lasting up to 84 days, crews had space motion sickness early in flight, moderate cardiovascular deconditioning, and loss of red cell mass and plasma volume. Calcium loss averaged 6 grams a month, or 0.5% of total body calcium, comparable to bed rest. Orthostatic intolerance appeared early after landing, and recovery was faster after missions with more in-flight exercise. The report concludes crews perform well with proper nutrition, regular exercise and enough sleep.
passages.tracking: Log exercise sessions and recovery after landing.

passages.title: Skylab clinical summary (Johnston & Dietlein, 1977)
passages.excerpt: Three Skylab crews flew for about 672, 1,427 and 2,017 hours. From a clinical view, all physiological and psychological responses were self-limiting or needed only minimal counteraction, and they did not rule out longer stays in zero gravity.
passages.tracking: Track whether each change settles without treatment.

passages.title: Early weightless flight (Mercury-Atlas 7) (NASA, 1962)
passages.excerpt: Medical examinations of two astronauts who each flew about 4.5 hours weightless found no physical or biochemical evidence of harm: no lung collapse (atelectasis), cosmic-ray damage or psychiatric problems. passages.title: Why spacewalk effort is monitored (Paul, 2012)
passages.excerpt: Tracking metabolic rate in real time during a spacewalk protects the crew member, shows how fast oxygen and cooling water are used, and lets planners change tasks. The laboratory method, open-circuit spirometry, is impractical in a suit. Heart rate, suit oxygen pressure decay and cooling-garment water temperatures have all been used, but none is reliable alone: heart rate also rises with stress, and oxygen decay includes suit leakage.

passages.title: Overexertion on Gemini spacewalks (Paul, 2012)
passages.excerpt: Gemini spacewalks took more effort than expected and at times exceeded the suit’s cooling. High exertion fogged the visor on Gemini IV and IX-A, and IX-A ended early. On Gemini XI sweat ran into the astronaut’s eyes and the spacewalk was ended early. For Gemini XII, NASA added restraints, underwater training and closer heart rate monitoring, advising the crew member when heart rate stayed at or above 140 beats per minute.

passages.title: Effort on the Apollo moonwalks (Paul, 2012)
passages.excerpt: Average metabolic rates on the 14 Apollo lunar surface spacewalks ranged from 780 to 1,200 Btu/hr, with a mean of about 930 Btu/hr (980 kJ/hr), lower than predicted. Moving equipment, climbing in and out of the lander and drilling cost the most, and riding the Lunar Roving Vehicle the least, about 392 Btu/hr. On Apollo 14 a crew member’s heart rate reached 150 bpm while hauling a cart toward Cone Crater, and the task was abandoned.

passages.title: Heart rate as a workload estimate (EVA dissertation, ch. 5)
passages.excerpt: In 132 Shuttle and ISS spacewalks of five hours or more, heart rate and metabolic rate fell together over the spacewalk, from about 117 bpm and 1,040 Btu/hr at the start to about 100 bpm and 813 Btu/hr at hour four. One regression across all spacewalks explained 40% of the variation, but one fitted to each crew member explained over 82% and kept prediction error within the 200 Btu/hr accepted during Apollo. On average each heartbeat corresponded to about 0.14 Btu.

passages.title: Simulated lunar spacewalks (EVA dissertation, ch. 6)
passages.excerpt: Two suited operators in NASA’s Mark III suit did 3- to 5-hour simulated lunar spacewalks at one-sixth gravity on NASA’s ARGOS offload rig, walking graded treadmills, sampling geology and moving objects.
